chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-Asadi narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Abi Imran narrated to us, saying: Abu Mus'ab Ahmad ibn Abi Bakr al-Zahri narrated to us, saying: Ali ibn Abi Ali al-Lahabi narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir from Jabir ibn Abdullah, who said: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said:

Indeed, what I fear most for my nation is unbridled desire (al-hawa) and prolonging of hope (tawil al-amal). As for unbridled desire, it turns one away from the truth; and as for prolonging of hope, it causes one to forget the Hereafter. This world has departed, moving away, and the Hereafter has arrived, moving forward. Each of them has its own children. If you are able to be among the children of the Hereafter and not among the children of the world, then do so. Indeed, today you are in a house of action and no reckoning, and tomorrow you will be in a house of reckoning and no action.

key_terms.الْهَوَى: Unbridled desire or whims that lead one away from truth
key_terms.دَارُ حِسَابٍ: House of reckoning (referring to the afterlife where deeds are judged)
key_terms.دَارُ عَمَلٍ: House of action (referring to the current life where deeds are performed)
key_terms.طُولُ الْأَمَلِ: Prolonging of hope (in worldly life), leading to negligence of the Hereafter

ai.seo_question: What are the two main dangers the Prophet warned his nation about regarding desire and hope?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Saduq highlights this hadith in *Al-Khisal* to illustrate the psychological barriers to spiritual success, framing 'hawa' (desire) and 'tul al-aml' (prolonged hope) as the primary causes of negligence. The metaphor of the world as a 'departing tent' and the Hereafter as an 'arriving tent' emphasizes the transient nature of worldly life, urging believers to prioritize eternal deeds over temporary comforts. This teaching underscores the Shia emphasis on active preparation for the final reckoning while still in the realm of free will.
